The use of recumbent length instead of stature in the assessment of body mass index (BM I) may lead to misclassification of children’s nutritional status, and this may be of particular relevance in overweight children.

1) there are differences between recumbent and standing length and height measurements in 2- and in 3-y-old girls and in 3 y-old boys; 2) these differences are small, but systematic and result in an upward shift in BMI, which is not reflected in current body mass index (BM)I reference charts; and 3) this small but systematic error can result in misinterpretations of individual BMI levels and trends
length and stature measurements are different in young children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of the European BMI references in children and adolescents.
the relevance of differences between recumbent and stature measurement in young children and its consequences for the comparison with BMI references.
the question of whether it is appropriate to use length instead of stature in children up to age 2 y.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the difference between length and stature measurement is of minor relevance in the interpretation of BMI values.
length should be preferred over stature in the measurement of young children.
stature measurements are preferred to length measurements for the assessment of growth in children aged 2-3 y.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
length is a more accurate measure of height than stature.
the use of the term ‘stature’ for the measurement of height is not appropriate in children under age 3 y, because of the difference between the length and the height of the child.
length and stature measurements are interchangeable for the use of BMI references in young children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when comparing length measurements with stature measurements, the difference between length and stature is small, but systematic and may lead to an upward shift of body mass index (BMIs).
the use of length in young children should be avoided and replaced with stature.
length measurements are preferred over stature measurements when using BMI references.
